Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

RiskMap 2.0.0

  • This version introduces many breaking changes from v1. The package should not be considered stable, but further breaking changes will be handled gracefully.
  • Test coverage has been increased from 0 to 92 %.
  • All functions have examples
  • Many functions have been renamed or removed:
v1 v2
assess_pp assess_prediction
assess_sim assess_simulation
check_mcmc plot_mcmc
compute_ID_coords create_ids
convex_hull_sf create_convex_hull
propose_utm propose_crs (chooses the CRS by its distortion of distances)
dast() Removed; will be replaced in a separate package
glgpm_sim simulate_glgpm
Laplace_sampling_MCMC Removed; the replacement is internal
matern.grad.phi matern_gradient_phi
matern.hessian.phi matern_hessian_phi
matern_cor matern_correlation
maxim.integrand maxim_integrand
plot_score / plot_AnPIT plot.RiskMap_cross_validation (the two are merged; by default it draws every plot the RiskMap_cross_validation object has data for)
plot_s_variogram plot.RiskMap_variogram
pred_over_grid predict
pred_target_grid predict
pred_target_shp predict with boundaries
set_control_sim set_control_mcmc
surf_sim simulate_glgpm
s_variogram variogram

Errors, warnings and messages

  • Every error, warning and message of RiskMap is raised through cli. Errors name the function that the user called, even when the problem is found deep inside it, and an input error describes the value supplied. Messages have been reworded to one style, with arguments, values and functions marked up. Code that matched the old wording of a message should match its class instead.
  • Conditions have classes, documented in ?riskmap_conditions, so that code can catch them by class rather than by their text. Every error RiskMap raises on purpose has class riskmap_error. An invalid argument has riskmap_error_input, whose field arg names the argument, a fit that fails riskmap_error_fit, and a state RiskMap should never reach riskmap_error_internal, which asks for a report. Warnings that a fit may not be reliable, such as an uncertified Monte Carlo error, have riskmap_warning_fit.
  • Errors from the compiled Langevin sampler are raised again as riskmap_error_fit, with the original error as the cause.
  • The messages argument of glgpm(), predict(), profile(), parametric_bootstrap(), check_fit(), assess_prediction() and assess_simulation() defaults to the option RiskMap.messages, as get_worldpop()’s does, so options(RiskMap.messages = FALSE) silences them all.
  • Some arguments are checked more strictly. glgpm() rejects a starting value of 0 for a variance of re() terms, and predict() rejects points with Z or M coordinates or empty points in newdata. match.arg() errors are replaced by RiskMap input errors, and a unique abbreviation is now accepted wherever a choice is made, as match.arg() allows.
  • Leaving out an argument that has no default gives a RiskMap input error that names the argument and the function, such as “object is missing, with no default.” from check_fit(), instead of R’s error where the argument is first used.
  • Messages start with a symbol, as the printed output does. Most have an information sign, a step done has a tick, such as a certified fit or a finished bootstrap, and something to note has an exclamation mark. glgpm() says in one message which coordinate reference system the model is fitted in and the units of distance. For data in longitude and latitude this is the message on their projection, which also says how to choose another.
  • A joint prediction in blocks warns once when the covariances of some blocks needed a diagonal jitter to be factorised, with how many blocks and the largest jitter, instead of once for each block.
  • get_worldpop() takes the default of messages from the option RiskMap.messages, so options(RiskMap.messages = FALSE) silences it.
  • A max_dist or phi that isn’t positive is now reported as “must be a single positive finite number” instead of “strictly between 0 and Inf”.

Progress

  • parametric_bootstrap(), profile(), assess_prediction() and assess_simulation() show a progress bar with the work done and an estimate of the time left, and predict() shows one while it predicts at many locations in blocks or propagates parameter uncertainty. glgpm() shows a line for each stage of Monte Carlo maximum likelihood, with the time the stage took. See ?riskmap_progress.
  • While a step of a fit runs in the console, its line has a spinner and the time so far, which move each time the likelihood is evaluated, so a long stage shows it is still running. This applies to the starting values from the Laplace approximation, each stage of Monte Carlo maximum likelihood, and the re-maximisation that profile() does before profiling. A step computed in one call to compiled code keeps a still line. These are the conditional samples drawn at the estimate, and the Langevin sampler that predict() runs when given control_mcmc, which now has a line of its own. A line too wide for the console is shortened so that its time still shows.
  • profile() shows its re-maximisation as a step in the console, and as the message it was before where progress is hidden.
  • Progress is shown when messages is TRUE and the option RiskMap.progress allows it. The option’s default is rlang::is_interactive(), so progress appears in the console but not in scripts, in documents rendered by knitr or in tests, even when these are started from the console. options(RiskMap.progress = TRUE) shows it in the log of a script, where a bar writes a line for each tenth of the work.
  • The bars replace the progress messages of the bootstrap (“k of n replicates done”), the profiles (“Profiling sigma2 (1 of 3)”), cross-validation (“Re-estimating model for subset i”) and simulation studies (“Simulation j of n”).
  • With cores above 1, the bootstrap and the profiles start one process per task, at most cores at a time, and collect each as it finishes, instead of dividing the tasks between the processes in advance. The results don’t change. A profile on several cores now also switches the main process to one BLAS thread while the workers run, as the bootstrap already did.

Printed output

  • The printed output of a fit, of its summary(), of check_fit() and of the summary of the checks is formatted with cli. Each starts with a rule that carries its title, the call is shown faint, and each verdict has a symbol. A certified fit and an OK check have a green tick, a check that needs care a yellow exclamation mark, and a problem a red cross. Hints have an information sign, and the fix of a check follows an arrow.
  • In a console that supports links, such as RStudio, the functions named in the printed output link to their help pages.
  • The output is still printed with cat(), not raised as messages, so it appears in knitr chunks with message: false and in capture.output(). Without colour support, as in knitr, it is plain text, and options(cli.unicode = FALSE) gives ASCII symbols, which a PDF without Unicode fonts needs.
  • Some printed wording changes. The certificate starts “Certified.” or “Not certified.” instead of “Certified:” or “Not certified:”, summary() gives the link in one sentence, such as “The canonical logit link.”, the log-likelihood and the AIC have no colon, and a fix follows an arrow instead of “Fix:”. Argument and function names in the findings and fixes of check_fit() are quoted with backticks, as in RiskMap’s messages. Code that matched the old printed text needs updating.
  • The printed checks give each status as its symbol instead of the words OK, SUSPICIOUS and PROBLEM, which stay in the column status of the element checks. Code that searched the printed checks for them should read that column.
  • RiskMap now needs cli 3.6.0 or later, for the links to help pages.
  • The summary() of a binomial, Poisson or negative binomial fit says where its starting values came from. Either they were given in start_pars, with RiskMap’s defaults for any not given, or they were all RiskMap’s defaults, or they came from a Gaussian fit to the transformed data, which glgpm() uses when the Laplace approximation of the likelihood prefers them. When the defaults were kept without that comparison, as for a model with re() terms or a link other than the canonical one, or after the comparison failed, the line says why. Before, a failure was recorded only in attr(fit, "starting_values")$fallback_reason. The choice is in the new element starting_values of mcml, and the reason in starting_reason. glgpm() no longer says “Using transformed-Gaussian automatic starting values.” when it makes that choice.
  • In a console with colours, the labels of rows that line up labels and values, such as the log-likelihood, the settings of a prediction or the evidence of check_fit(), are grey, so that the values stand out.
  • Printing the result of assess_prediction() gives the models, the test sets, how the parameters were set and the scores averaged over the test sets, instead of the whole list of scores and test sets. Its summary() gives the averages and the scores of each test set as tables, instead of a line for each score.
  • The summary of parametric_bootstrap(), the profiles of profile(), the variogram of variogram() and the distances of summarise_distance() are printed in the same style. The variogram also says in how many distance classes it lies outside the envelope.
  • Predictions, models for simulation, simulations and assessments of simulations are printed in the same style. A model for simulation names its link as a fit does, and gives its parameters one per line. The summary of an assessment of simulations gives each spatial scale a rule of its own, and a failed model fit becomes a warning bullet.
  • The result of predict() records the link of its fit, when it is not the canonical one, in the new element link, so that its print names the link as the print of the fit does.
  • The summary() of a fit gives the parameters of its family, such as the measurement error variance of a Gaussian model, in the element family_parameters, a table of those that were estimated, and in held_family_parameters, a list of those held at a given value, such as fix_var_me. They replace the element me, which held either. So to_table() of a fit with fix_var_me no longer adds a row that repeats the fixed value in every column, and the row of the intercept of a fit with no covariates is named “(Intercept)”, where it was blank.

Datasets

  • Apart from liberia, all datasets are now in an simple features (sf) format.
  • anopheles is now in WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N (EPSG:32632), where it was in Pseudo-Mercator (EPSG:3857), and italy_sim in WGS 84 / UTM zone 33N (EPSG:32633), where it was in UTM zone 34N. The old CRSs distorted distances by up to 1.0% and 1.4% over the data, and the new ones by less than 0.1% and 0.5%. Distances, and so fits, variograms and grids made from these datasets, change slightly. Pseudo-Mercator is also not conformal, so it stretched distances more north-south than east-west.

Coordinate reference systems

  • Datasets must have a coordinate reference system. When coordinates are in latitude/longitude and model_crs is not supplied, they are now automatically reprojected to the CRS from propose_crs(). predict(), simulate_glgpm() and assess_prediction() have been updated to match; simulate_glgpm()’s own convert_to_crs/scale_to_km arguments have likewise been replaced with model_crs/distance_units.
  • providing model_crs in longitude/latitude now raises an error.
  • The new propose_crs() chooses the projected CRS that distorts distances least over the data. It compares the WGS 84 UTM zone at the centre of the data and its two neighbours with four conformal projections centred on the data (oblique stereographic, transverse Mercator, oblique Mercator and Lambert conformal conic), whose parameters minimise the largest scale error over the region. It returns the EPSG code of the best UTM zone when that zone distorts distances by at most 0.5% (epsg_tolerance), and otherwise a crs object for the best centred projection, named “RiskMap …” in its WKT. The new crs_distortion() measures the distortion of any projected CRS over the data.
  • glgpm(), summarise_distance(), variogram(), create_grid() and specify_glgpm() now project data in longitude and latitude with propose_crs(). Earlier development versions used the UTM zone holding most locations, which could distort distances by more than 3%, for example over the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the CRS now chosen distorts them by less than 0.5%. Data that a UTM zone covers well get the zone at their centre, which may differ from the zone used before. Fits, distances and grids of data in longitude and latitude can therefore change. Set model_crs or distance_crs, or project the data first, to keep a given CRS. The message names the CRS and the units of distance, and says how to choose another CRS. It doesn’t give the distortion, which the warning below reports when it is above 1%, and which crs_distortion() measures for any CRS.
  • These functions warn, with class riskmap_warning_crs, when the CRS used, whether given, carried by the data or chosen, distorts distances by more than 1% over the data. When no planar CRS can do better, as over sub-Saharan Africa, the warning says so.
  • propose_utm() has been removed. Use propose_crs(), which returns the same UTM zone for data that a zone covers well. propose_utm() took the zone holding most locations, which could be far from the centre of the data.
  • In glgpm(), convert_to_crs has been replaced with model_crs and scale_to_km has been replaced with distance_units ("km" or "m").

Exploratory analysis

  • plot() for variogram() results gains show_pairs (default FALSE), which labels each point with the number of pairs of locations in its distance class, so that unstable semivariances from few pairs can be recognised.
  • plot() for variogram() results draws the semivariances as points without joining lines, omits distance classes without pairs (which previously caused “Removed rows” warnings), starts both axes at zero, uses theme_minimal() as other RiskMap plots do, and draws in red the points that fall outside the envelope. plot_envelope is now checked.
  • variogram() results gain a print() method that reports the distance classes and the envelope settings before the table.
  • summarise_distance() results gain a print() method that shows the distances to three significant digits (set by digits), with the number of unique locations and the distance units. The values are still stored in full.
  • In summarise_distance() and variogram(), scale_to_km has been replaced with distance_units ("km" or "m"), for consistency with glgpm(). Both now default to "km", as glgpm() does. For variogram() this changes the default from "m", so code that gives breaks or max_dist in metres should set distance_units = "m".
  • variogram() accepts breaks or max_dist beyond the largest distance between locations, and warns only when whole distance classes lie beyond it. When no pair falls in any class, the error reports the range of the distances instead of always suggesting a change of units. max_dist = NULL can be passed together with breaks.
  • variogram() no longer fails when the envelope is built for a single distance class, and runs about twice as fast with 2,000 or more locations, with identical results. Rounding error no longer makes the envelope exclude one curve too few at some levels, such as 0.9 with 999 permutations. The default level of 0.95 with 999 permutations was not affected.
  • In summarise_distance() and variogram(), convert_to_utm has been replaced with distance_crs, matching glgpm()’s model_crs convention: an already-projected CRS is retained as-is, longitude/latitude data is automatically reprojected to an appropriate UTM zone with a message, and an explicitly supplied distance_crs must be projected. Distances now correctly account for the CRS’s native linear units rather than assuming metres.
  • variogram() now uses a simultaneous extreme-rank-length permutation envelope instead of separate pointwise intervals. It remains an exploratory diagnostic and does not report a hypothesis-test p-value. Its pairwise permutation engine is compiled, distances and lag bins are computed once, and the default is 999 permutations plus the observed curve. The returned columns are now distance, semivariance, n_pairs, lower_envelope and upper_envelope. A seed can be supplied without changing the caller’s random-number state. plot_variogram() (now plot.RiskMap_variogram()) shows the envelope by default and warns when it was omitted with n_permutations = 0.
  • The bins parameter in variogram() has been removed and replaced with breaks.

Model fitting

  • glgpm() fits negative binomial models of overdispersed counts, with family = negative_binomial(), the log link and the exposure in denominator. The size theta is estimated, starting from the negative binomial regression without random effects or from start_pars$theta, unless it is given, as in negative_binomial(theta = 2) or MASS::negative.binomial(2), at which it is held. A size that goes to the Poisson limit is held there and reported by check_fit(). An estimated size can’t be fitted with a nugget or a random effect with one level per observation when there is one observation per location. predict(), simulate_glgpm(), specify_glgpm(), assess_prediction(), profile(), parametric_bootstrap() and check_fit() take the size of a fit, and maxim_integrand() takes the family with its size. Its log-likelihood leaves out the same terms as that of a Poisson fit, so the two can be compared.

  • Several re() calls in a formula are now combined, so re(a) + re(b) is the same model as re(a, b). Previously only the last call was fitted, with no warning. A second, different gp() term, which also used to replace the first with no warning, is now an error.

  • A second offset() term, which used to be ignored with no warning, is now an error. offset() must name a column of data, and an expression such as offset(log(n)) now stops with a message that says so. An offset is also read correctly when the formula has several re() calls.

  • Breaking change: the seed has moved out of set_control_mcmc(), whose seed argument is removed. glgpm(), predict(), assess_prediction() and assess_simulation() take a seed argument instead, as simulate_glgpm(), variogram() and profile() already did. Replacing control_mcmc = set_control_mcmc(seed = s) with seed = s gives identical results. Without a seed, glgpm() draws one from the session’s random number generator, so set.seed() before the call reproduces the fit, and two calls in a row differ. The seed used is returned as seed in the fitted object, and glgpm(..., seed = fit$seed) reproduces any binomial or Poisson fit, including its final conditional samples.

  • The den argument in glgpm() has been renamed to denominator.

  • glpgm() now only accepts data in an sf format. Consequently the locations do not need to be passed to gp() when fitting a model as they are included automatically.

  • The nugget parameter in gp() is now FALSE by default and should be set to TRUE to estimate it.

  • Canonical binomial and Poisson models now use compiled likelihood and MALA kernels. The implementation retains the existing sampler, including support for nugget effects and multiple unstructured random effects, while avoiding the main interpreted-R bottlenecks. Custom inverse-link functions continue to use the general R implementation.

  • plot_mcmc() draws its diagnostics with ggplot2 and patchwork and returns them as a patchwork object, instead of drawing with base graphics and resetting par(). By default it shows the trace plot and the autocorrelation function of the mean of the spatial random effects and of the location with the smallest effective sample size, with a histogram of the effective sample sizes at all the locations. The trace plots show the iterations at which the samples were kept, so fits now record the n_sim, burnin and thin of their samples in attr(fit, "mcmc"). component now defaults to the location with the smallest effective sample size, can select several locations and can be given together with check_mean = TRUE. The mean and component previously included the levels of unstructured random effects, which are stored after the locations in S_samples. They now refer to the locations only.

  • The new summarise_mcmc() returns a tibble of the effective sample sizes of the mean of the spatial random effects, of each location and of each level of an unstructured random effect. They are computed with the initial monotone sequence estimator of Geyer (1992), so the package no longer depends on sns. patchwork has moved from Suggests to Imports.

  • Non-Gaussian optimisation now reuses the sample-wise Monte Carlo log integrand when the objective, gradient, and Hessian are evaluated at identical parameters, avoiding a repeated likelihood calculation.

  • profile() computes profile likelihoods of binomial and Poisson models fitted by certified Monte Carlo maximum likelihood, for single parameters and for pairs, on one fixed bank of draws so that the profiles are smooth. It reports profile and Wald intervals and says if a point on a profile is higher than the estimate. Marginal grids of 11 points are extended with doubling steps where the profile is flat, up to 11 points a side, and an end the profile does not reach is reported as open. Interval ends are interpolated in the signed root of the deviance, with one more point at a crossing between distant points, and the points around each end are also solved from the estimate, because constrained maxima can be multimodal. The constrained maximisations work on the scale of the fit, with standardised covariates, which avoids the false convergence that coefficients of covariates with large ranges caused in their own units, and each starts from the extrapolation of the two previous solutions. One that still stops with a non-zero code is solved again with a central-difference gradient. A fixed coefficient whose constraint the start cannot meet within the bounds is first moved to the nearest feasible point, and each point records whether it was solved, is infeasible or failed. Joint profiles are computed only when pairs asks for them, and the time left is estimated as the profiles run. With cores above one, the two sides of each profile, the ends of the intervals and the joint profiles run in parallel by forking (not on Windows), with the same results as on one core with one BLAS thread. plot() draws the marginal profiles against their quadratic approximation and the joint profiles as confidence regions with the marginal ridges, as a corner plot for one pair.

  • profile() also computes profile likelihoods of linear geostatistical (Gaussian) models, from their exact likelihood, so n_draws and seed are not used. Every estimated parameter can be profiled: the regression coefficients, the spatial variance and scale, the variance of the nugget (tau2, as summary() reports it, rather than its ratio to the spatial variance), the measurement error variance unless it is fixed, and the variances of the random effects, with the labels of summary(). For each value of the covariance parameters the coefficients are found by generalised least squares, and models with more than three observations per latent effect use the Woodbury identity, as glgpm() does. The ends of the profile intervals are refined until the deviance of a solved point is within 0.01 of the cut-off, grid steps of the variances and the scale are at most 1 on the log scale, so that a variance estimated near zero, with a huge standard error, is still profiled, and each point of a joint profile is also solved from the estimate, since a neighbour’s solution with a variance near zero can leave the optimiser on a plateau. A variance that the data cannot tell from zero has a profile that stays below the cut-off down to its lower bound, and its interval is reported as open there. The smoothness kappa stays fixed and can be profiled by refitting over fixed values.

  • In plot() of a profile, the subtitle of each marginal panel gives the estimate, the profile interval and the Wald interval on separate lines, so that it is no longer cut off in panels half or a third of a page wide, and the two entries of the ridge legend of a joint profile are stacked.

  • Non-Gaussian models are now fitted by certified Monte Carlo maximum likelihood. The estimated likelihood is maximised on a fitting sample of 1,000 draws, the estimate is corrected by one Newton step with the score from an independent validation sample of 5,000 draws, and the corrected estimate is certified with a second, fresh validation sample. The certificate is an approximate 95% bound, in statistical standard errors, on the Monte Carlo error of the estimate at the maximum found. When it exceeds the tolerance (0.1 by default), both samples are enlarged to the size predicted to meet it, up to max_samples. The importance distribution is a Gaussian approximation fitted to the whole conditional distribution of the latent effects (efficient importance sampling), which keeps far more draws effective than the Laplace approximation in sparse data. Binomial and Poisson models, with or without a nugget and unstructured random effects, share one implementation, and the Laplace approximation remains as a fallback and as an option. If the global proposal fails while an estimate is being corrected or certified, the stage is repeated with the Laplace proposal on fresh draws, so that every certificate rests on validation draws taken after everything that led to it. set_control_mcml() gains validation_samples, tolerance and proposal, and loses min_effective_samples, max_pareto_k, max_mcse_ratio and score_probability. The defaults of max_samples and max_stages are now 16,000 and 4. Fitted objects report mcml_certified in place of mcml_converged.

  • Certified MCML continues the Newton correction when one step leaves a residual. Where the log-likelihood is far from quadratic between the fitted estimate and the maximum, as along a spatial variance close to zero, one Newton step stops short of the maximum, and the certificate, measured in the curvature at the fitted estimate, sees only part of the shortfall. The fitting sample now predicts the residual of the first step, at the cost of one gradient on that sample, and when it exceeds a quarter of the validation sample’s radius, further Newton steps are taken with the score from the same validation sample, each in the fitting sample’s curvature at the current point, until a step is below a tenth of the radius (at most four more steps). The estimate is then certified in the curvature at the last step. If the steps stop short by more than the certificate tolerates, they are discarded, the stage is not certified, and the next stage starts from the estimate of the first step. The check does not act where the validation sample’s radius is below 1e-6 statistical standard errors, as when the spatial variance is held at zero and the likelihood is exact, because the predicted residual is then the rounding error of the differences divided by the radius. Fits where the check does not fire are unchanged. Where it fires, the estimate and the certificate change, and so do the returned standard errors, which now come from the curvature at the last step. On a simulated survey with a log spatial variance of -4.56 at the maximum, the standard error of the log variance moved from 14.5 to 29.5, against 30.2 at the maximum. Each stage of mcml_history records the predicted residual and the number of Newton steps.

  • Certified MCML distinguishes Monte Carlo error from weak identification. A variance component estimated as zero (and the spatial scale when the spatial variance is zero) is held at the boundary, the first stage is restarted once from an interior value, and precision is assessed on the remaining parameters, which keep their standard errors. A spatial scale estimated below the median distance between neighbouring locations is reported as estimated, with a warning that gives its practical range, explains that such a scale may be weakly identified, points to its profile likelihood and suggests a nugget model, a fixed scale or the PC prior. If the information matrix is still singular, fitting stops instead of drawing more samples. Each case produces a plain-language warning.

  • Certified MCML recognises data whose likelihood has no maximum, which previously could be certified with a regression coefficient at the bound of the search. When no observation has a positive, when every individual tested is positive, or more generally when the covariates separate the data (for example, a category of a factor whose locations have no positives), the likelihood increases without limit as some coefficients tend to infinity. An exact check of the data finds such a separation before the fit, and a coefficient that reaches the bound of the search is treated in the same way. The fit then ends with the outcome “no maximum”, without standard errors or certificate, and a warning names the cause and the covariates involved. On a simulated survey with no positives among 5,000 individuals tested, six of ten runs had been certified with an intercept of -30 and a standard error of about 23,500. Surveys with at least one positive in each such category keep a finite maximum and are fitted as before.

  • A binomial fit whose covariate separates the data completely, such as one where every location with a positive covariate has only positives and every other location none, now ends with the outcome “no maximum” as intended. It stopped with “the estimated log-likelihood is not finite at the optimum”, although the separation had been found. With the logit link, the linear predictor of a location where every individual is positive passes 36.74 well inside the bounds of the search, the inverse logit rounds to 1 there, and the formulas of the conditional mode of the latent effects divided zero by zero. The canonical links now use the exact form of each observation’s log-likelihood, score and curvature where the probability rounds to 0 or 1 or the mean of a count underflows to 0, in the fit and in maxim_integrand(). The probit and complementary log-log links already ended such fits with “no maximum”. Fits that never reach these limits are unchanged, since the new forms apply only where the previous ones could not be evaluated.

  • maxim_integrand() now takes denominator instead of units_m, matching glgpm(). Its documentation no longer lists the Gaussian family, which it has never supported, and describes the Newton-type optimisation it actually uses.

  • Removed unused internal helpers (log_mean_exp(), importance_effective_sample_size(), restore_spatial_range()) and the compiled kernel cpp_canonical_likelihood(), which no longer had callers.

  • set_control_mcml() gains pc_prior (default FALSE) and its thresholds pc_sigma_threshold, pc_sigma_probability, pc_scale_threshold and pc_scale_probability. When pc_prior = TRUE, the spatial variance and scale are penalised by penalised-complexity priors (by default P(sigma > 1) = 0.05 and P(phi < median nearest-neighbour distance) = 0.05), which stabilises estimation in small or low-prevalence surveys. Warnings about a spatial variance estimated as zero, a small spatial scale or a singular information matrix now suggest this option.

  • The final conditional sampling in glgpm() (used for fitted values and stored prediction samples) now uses the compiled MALA kernel for canonical links, as intended. It previously passed the inverse-link function itself, which selected the general R implementation with numerical derivatives; a binomial fit to the liberia data now takes about 2 s instead of 27 s. Fresh conditional runs in predict() now honour a custom inverse link.

  • set_control_mcml() gains laplace_start (default TRUE), which maximises the Laplace approximation from the starting values before MCML.

  • set_control_mcml() gains check_maxima (default TRUE). The certificate establishes Monte Carlo precision at the maximum found, and in sparse surveys an optimiser can stop at a maximum with a spatial scale far below the spacing between locations while a higher one exists at a longer scale. When the fitted scale is below half the median distance between neighbouring locations, the fit is repeated from four dispersed starting values on the same draws. Candidates within 0.1 standard errors of each other are treated as one maximum, and separate maxima are compared on independent draws. A message says when and why the check runs, and a warning says when it moves the estimate to another maximum or finds two maxima that fit about equally well. The check does not prove that no higher maximum exists.

  • The check for other maxima also looks at short scales after a fit at a long one. The likelihood with independent location effects, the limit of the model as the spatial scale goes to zero, is computed exactly by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature and maximised once per survey. The estimated likelihood is evaluated at four scales from an eighth of the spacing between neighbouring locations to the spacing, with the coefficients and variance of that limit and one three-point step in the log variance where the value is close, and the fit is repeated from the best point if it comes within 0.25 log-likelihood units of the fit or if an evaluation fails. The limit and Jensen lower bounds at those scales are exact, and if one of them exceeds the fitted log-likelihood, estimated on independent draws, a further search is forced and a warning is given if it does not resolve the alarm. A fit whose scale reaches the point where the correlation between the closest locations is below 1e-6 ends with the outcome “numerically independent”, without standard errors or certificate, since the fit is then one of independent location effects and the spatial scale is unresolved. A fit at a short positive scale whose likelihood is not clearly above the limit at the current Monte Carlo precision is assessed as usual, with a warning that points to profile() for the scale. Separate maxima whose comparison on independent draws is ambiguous are compared again on four times as many draws, and that comparison serves every later one. A stage whose global proposal fails at its start goes straight to the Laplace proposal, instead of being completed and then discarded, and the factorisation of the spatial covariance is reused while only the regression coefficients change. The screen and the exact bounds need the canonical links and no unstructured random effects, and other models keep the earlier check.

  • Certified MCML computes the importance weights (for the canonical binomial and Poisson links) and the dense linear algebra of the proposal in compiled code, with the same LAPACK and BLAS routines R uses, and gives results identical to the previous R code (up to the last bits on platforms whose compilers fuse multiply and add). A fit no longer creates several large temporary matrices at every evaluation of the likelihood, whose garbage collection took about half of a fit.

  • Fitted models have a print() method, which gives the call, the estimates of the regression coefficients and covariance parameters on their natural scale, the log-likelihood and, for binomial and Poisson models, whether the Monte Carlo error of the estimate is certified. Printing a fit previously listed every component of the object, including the data. summary() of a binomial or Poisson fit now reports the certificate (its bound in statistical standard errors, the level of the bound, the tolerance, the number of stages and the draws at the last stage), with short notes on what the warnings of the fit reported and the advice they gave, so that both are available for a saved model. The certificate is in the mcml component of the summary.

  • The messages and warnings of certified MCML quote the spatial scale of the returned estimate, after the Newton correction. The message that announces the refits from dispersed starting values, which are decided before the correction, now says that it quotes the scale of the first fit, before its correction. When the repeated Newton correction does not converge at the last stage, the warning says so, instead of describing the bound as above the tolerance.

  • A failure of the global importance distribution no longer condemns the whole fit. In sparse data the Laplace estimate can have a very large nugget, where the fixed-point iteration stalls and whether it converges can depend on rounding, while it converges quickly elsewhere. A failure at the Laplace estimate now restarts the first stage from the starting values with the global importance distribution, and a stage that does fall back to the Laplace approximation is followed by one that tries the global distribution again. Fits without a failure are unchanged. mcml_history records why the iteration failed.

  • New check_fit() goes through the checks on how a model was computed, says which are OK and which need a look, and gives the fix where there is one. Its plot() method shows the certificate, the effective draws, the Pareto shape and the changes in the estimates by stage. It reports what used to crowd the output, including the effective draws and Pareto shape of the certification draws, a heavy tail of the importance weights, changes of importance distribution and a search for the conditional mode that stopped at its iteration limit.

  • Certified MCML is quieter. A fit warns only about what changes how a result is read, which is a certificate that is missing or above the tolerance, a likelihood without a maximum, weak identification, other maxima and a spatial variance at zero, in a sentence or two that point to check_fit(). A nugget or random effect at zero, a short spatial scale and a scale close to the limit of independent effects no longer warn. With messages = TRUE a certified fit gives one line. summary() ends with the verdict and the number of checks that need a look, in place of its notes, and summary()$mcml$notes is replaced by checks_to_review.

  • Certified MCML now tests a nugget or random-effect variance that it holds at zero. A fit moves in the log of a variance, whose gradient vanishes near zero whatever the slope in the variance itself, so reaching the boundary does not show that zero is a maximum. The slope at zero is estimated on an independent bank of draws. If it is clearly positive the stage is not certified, because the held point is not a maximum, and the next stage starts the variance from an interior value, even at the largest number of draws if stages remain. If it is clearly negative, check_fit() reports that zero is the maximum and the variance no longer counts as a check that needs a look. Fits that hold no variance are unchanged, and those with a custom link are not tested.

  • The radius of the certificate, its allowance for the Monte Carlo error of the certification sample’s own score, is now the larger of that sample’s radius and the radius of a replicate of it, with the same number of draws at the same estimate on a stream of its own. The radius of one sample is estimated from its own draws, and it is too small when the sample misses the rare draws of very large weight that dominate its error. On 13 simulated binomial surveys with 500 samples of 5,000 draws each, how often the error that the radius allows for exceeded it fell from at most 6.7% to at most 2.9%, against the 5% the radius is meant to hold, and how often the Monte Carlo error of the estimate exceeded the certificate fell from at most 0.62% to at most 0.20%. On 16 simulated Poisson surveys the first fell from at most 10.0% to at most 4.6%. The certificate changes for every fit, and the replicate costs about 9% more fit time. In 1,270 paired fits of 127 simulated binomial surveys every fit stayed certified, the median certificate grew from 0.0171 to 0.0175 statistical standard errors, and 12 more fits needed a second stage. check_fit() says which sample set the radius in the radius_from column of its stages table, and each stage of mcml_history records both radii (certificate_radii) and the replicate’s weight diagnostics (replicate_validation).

  • With a nugget and the spatial variance at zero, the exact alarm of the check for other maxima now also tries scales up to 16 times the spacing, with 2% to 30% of the total variance in the spatial effect, and fires when a lower bound on the likelihood is above the maximum of the model with independent location effects by more than half the squared tolerance. The screen stopped at the spacing and only tried a share near zero, which could miss a spatial effect that a large nugget was absorbing.

  • Certified MCML now fits custom inverse links that reach the limits of their range or are not log-concave, which previously stopped with “no valid fit”. A probability that rounds to exactly one, as cloglog does from a linear predictor of 3.6 and probit from 8.3, set the likelihood of every draw in the bank to zero. Such a draw now keeps a finite likelihood, with each failure charged at the bound of 2^-53, and the other draws are unaffected. The conditional mode is found where the likelihood is convex, as it is for the link of an imperfect test, and the curvature no longer underflows far into a tail. Final conditional sampling no longer rejects a proposal whose probability rounds to one, which cut off the samples at sites where every trial was positive. A custom link that returns a value that is not a number, or is outside the range of the family, anywhere from -50 to 50 is now refused when it is supplied. Fits with the canonical links are unchanged.

  • A custom inverse link now gets the checks of the canonical links. A nugget or random-effect variance held at zero is tested by its slope there, and the check for other maxima runs its screen of short scales and its exact alarms, which take the link’s terms in the likelihood with independent location effects. Neither test needs the link to be log-concave. The sampler of the final latent draws and the sampler behind predictions with parameter uncertainty now receive the derivatives that the fit used, in place of deriving them again from the inverse link. Errors while an importance distribution is built at a trial parameter value, which give that value no weight, are counted and reported by check_fit(). Fits with the canonical links are unchanged.

  • The likelihood with independent location effects, behind the screen of short scales and the exact alarms, is now right at every location for a custom link. It integrated each location’s effect by Gauss-Hermite quadrature at a mode found by Newton steps from zero. Where a probability rounds to one, as for cloglog from a linear predictor of 3.6 and probit from 8.3, the likelihood of a location with a failure is flat, the search did not move, and the value could be wrong by several log units without the change from 30 to 60 nodes showing it. With a link that is not log-concave, such as that of an imperfect test, the search could stop at a lower mode. A custom link now takes the rule of the site table, the trapezium rule over the whole range where the integrand is not negligible, which assumes no mode, and its recorded error is the change when the step is doubled. Fits with the canonical links are unchanged.

  • A failure of the global proposal while the check for other maxima evaluates the likelihood far from the fitted maximum, as at the short scales of its screen, no longer makes the stage repeat with the Laplace proposal. That evaluation already uses the Laplace proposal at its own parameter values, and the failure says nothing about the proposal at the maximum. Since the screen runs for custom links, such failures in it made the first stage of a cauchit fit of loaloa repeat with the Laplace proposal, which suits that link far worse, and the fit was no longer certified. It is now certified at its first stage, with the global proposal. The failures still count when the check keeps the maximum of one of its refits, which is then the fit of the stage. Fits without such a failure are unchanged.

  • A refit of the global proposal in which a location’s quadratic fit has too few weighted quadrature nodes is now a failed refit for the canonical links too, as it already was for custom links, so the stage repeats with the Laplace proposal. It stopped inside the proposal with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, which gave the trial parameter value no weight. The case arises when the proposal for a location with many tests lies many widths of its likelihood away from it, as in refits from an anchor where the spatial variance is near zero. A fit started there could not leave that variance, reported it as effectively zero and certified only the regression coefficients, at a log-likelihood 240 units below the maximum it now reaches. No fit in the package’s tests reaches this case, nor do fits of surveys from Liberia, Loa loa, Malawi and Tanzania, and those fits are unchanged.

  • A custom inverse link that Deriv cannot differentiate, such as a bare invlink = pnorm, now has its derivatives computed for all values at once. They were computed one value at a time, which made such a fit much slower than the same link written as function(eta) pnorm(eta).

  • The numerical derivatives of a custom inverse link that Deriv cannot differentiate are now accurate near a linear predictor of zero. Their steps were relative to the linear predictor down to 1.8e-5, so just above it they fell to about 2e-9, and the second derivative, the numerical derivative of the first, was wrong by up to about 2,000 for linear predictors between about 2e-5 and 1e-2 (-40 at 1e-4 for function(eta) 0.01 + 0.89 * plogis(eta), where it is -1.1e-5). No step is now below 1e-4, and the steps are unchanged where the linear predictor is at least 1 in absolute value. The second derivative enters the curvature of the mode search and of the proposals but not the importance weights, so estimates were valid, but fits with such a link took a different path.

  • A custom inverse link built from plogis, pt or pcauchy, such as function(eta) 0.01 + 0.89 * plogis(eta) for an imperfect test or function(eta) pt(eta, 4), and a bare invlink = pnorm, plogis, pcauchy or exp, now has exact derivatives, as a link built from pnorm or exp already had. Deriv has no rules for these functions and cannot read the compiled body of a bare function, so their derivatives were numerical. Numerical derivatives are accurate but not smooth, and the search for starting values by the Laplace approximation, which differences the approximation, could stop short of its maximum. A call of these functions with a location, scale, tail or logarithm other than the default is still differentiated numerically. A link built inside another function, such as make_link <- function(sens) function(eta) 0.01 + sens * plogis(eta), is now differentiated exactly too, where its derivatives were numerical because they could not find the link’s own variables. In 31 paired fits every outcome was the same and the starting values were better in 24 of 30 and worse in none, and plogis given as a function now reproduces the fits of the canonical logit link to within 1e-6 standard errors.

  • With a link not known to make the likelihood log-concave, cauchit or an inverse link given in invlink, the global proposal now floors the curvature of its factors smoothly at the bound that keeps its precision positive definite, so that the proposal depends smoothly on the curvatures, as the certificate assumes of its dependence on the parameters. The floor had a kink where it starts to act, which it does in nearly every refit under cauchit and the imperfect test. The bound comes from the smallest eigenvalue of the prior precision, which keeps a kink where the smallest eigenvalues of two of its blocks cross, as with re() terms. The eigenvalue is now computed once for each value of the covariance parameters, where cauchit computed it for every proposal and a link given as a function did not need it. Fits with the logit, probit, cloglog and log links are unchanged. In 56 paired fits every certified fit kept its certificate and its stages, and its estimates moved by at most 2e-6 standard errors.

  • With integrate_noise, the global proposal’s iteration now converges where the curvature of a factor is small. It floored the candidates of its acceleration with the same smooth floor as its refits, which moves a value it has already floored, so wherever a curvature was below about 0.0115 the iteration could not reach its tolerance, stopped at its limit of 500 refits and was accepted as a stalled anchor. This happened in 70 of 171 integrated fits measured, among them every fit of the Tanzania survey with a nugget, and under integrate_noise = "auto" it went unrecorded in stages fitted in the sampled form. The candidates are now floored with pmax() at zero, as those of links not known to be log-concave are floored at their bound, so the proposal is the same fixed point, now reached in a median of 9 refits. In the paired fits no iteration stalled, and every certified fit stayed certified in the same stages with its certificate within 1.3%. The estimates of certified fits moved by at most 2.5e-4 standard errors, apart from three fits of one survey whose spatial variance was held at its limit and one under an imperfect test (up to 0.08). Imperfect-test fits that certified in neither version moved more, by up to 0.25 standard errors on a simulated survey at 5% prevalence and up to 5.6 on degenerate ones, as much as a new seed moves them, and one of them was reported as weakly identified after one stage rather than as having no maximum after two. A global iteration that stops just short of its tolerance is still accepted.

  • Fits with the probit, cloglog or cauchit link named in family, such as family = binomial("probit"), now compute their importance weights in compiled code, as the canonical logit and log links do. Each weight takes half the time it did in R, and such fits are 1.3 to 1.8 times faster on surveys of 200 to 400 sites, from 90 to 65 seconds for probit on the Tanzania survey of 387 sites and from 29 to 16 minutes for a cauchit fit that needs two stages. The compiled weights repeat the R computation operation for operation, so fits are unchanged (to the last bit on x86-64). An inverse link given as a function in invlink still computes its weights in R.

  • glgpm(), specify_glgpm() and maxim_integrand() now take a family object in family, as glm() does, so a link can be named as in family = binomial("probit"). Binomial models take the logit, probit, cloglog and cauchit links, Poisson models the log link and Gaussian models the identity link, and family = binomial is read as binomial(). The logit and log links fit exactly as family = "binomial" and family = "poisson" do. A named link gives the estimates of its inverse supplied in invlink, with exact derivatives, so it is never differentiated during the fit and is faster than an inverse such as a bare pnorm. binomial("log") and poisson("identity"), whose means can leave the range of the family, poisson("sqrt"), whose inverse is not monotone, quasi families, which have no likelihood, and other families are refused with a message pointing to invlink, which still takes any other inverse link as a function. A link given both in family and in invlink is an error, and invlink does not take the name of a link. print() and summary() name the link, and simulations, cross-validation refits and the parametric bootstrap keep it. The undocumented list form of invlink now takes only inv, d1 and d2, and specify_glgpm() no longer accepts an abbreviated family such as "bin", as glgpm() never did. summary() writes an inverse link taken from a package, such as a bare invlink = pnorm, by its name instead of its compiled body, .Call(C_pnorm, ...).

  • check_fit() adds a row when a link is not known to make the likelihood of each location log-concave in its latent effect, as the cauchit link and links given as a function in invlink are not, since the latent effects can then have more than one conditional mode. The row is OK, because this belongs to the model and not to how it was fitted. A fit with a named link takes its starting regression coefficients from a binomial regression with that link instead of a logit regression, and falls back on the logit regression if that one cannot be fitted.

  • The row “Link” of check_fit() also says when it has not been measured on simulated surveys how often the radius of the bound on the Monte Carlo error is too small, as it has for the logit and probit links of binomial data and the log link of Poisson and negative binomial counts, and points to check_fit(extra = "radius"), which predicts it for the fit. A fit with the cloglog link, which makes the likelihood log-concave, now has the row for that reason. For a link given as a function in invlink, the row says where the log-likelihood of a record was found to be convex on a grid of linear predictors from -30 to 30, so that a link such as that of an imperfect test is known not to be log-concave.

  • A binomial model fitted without an intercept, such as y ~ 0 + x1 + x2 + gp(), now takes its automatic starting regression coefficients from a regression without an intercept. The start regression dropped the first column of the design matrix and added an intercept, so the starting coefficients were shifted by one column, and the first covariate started from the intercept of another model. With the logit link the transformed-Gaussian start usually replaced them, but with a named link such as probit, or a link given in invlink, MCML started from them. In simulated surveys this made fits with a nugget up to ten times slower, and with laplace_start = FALSE it led one fit to a lower maximum. Fits of models with an intercept are unchanged.

  • glgpm() no longer compares automatic starting values for a binomial, Poisson or negative binomial model with re() terms, and starts it from RiskMap’s defaults, as it always did in effect. The other start came from a Gaussian model of the transformed records whose covariance was over all the records, or over all the levels of the terms, and both starts were scored with a dense matrix over all the latent effects. On simulated surveys of eight households at each of 50, 100 and 150 locations, a fit took 77, 403 and 736 seconds with the comparison and 24, 35 and 12 seconds without it. On larger surveys the comparison could ask for gigabytes at once, so whether a fit compared the starts or fell back to the defaults depended on the memory available. It also could never choose the other start, because the Laplace approximation at that start carried the name of the re() term and was read as missing. Fits of models with re() terms are unchanged.

  • Without re() terms, the Gaussian model that gives the other automatic start is fitted to one observation per location, the totals of the location where it has several records, with the covariates averaged over its records. Its covariance was over all the records, so at 1,000 locations with three records each the comparison took 407 seconds against 80 for the fit, and now takes 32. A survey with one record per location is fitted exactly as before. With several records at a location the other start changes, and the empirical logit of a total follows the proportion at the location, where that of a binary record is always log(3) or -log(3).

  • Certified MCML now builds every global proposal of a stage, other than the one at its start, from three plain refits of the factors found at the start, in place of iterating with Anderson acceleration until no factor moves by more than 1e-8. The stopping rule of the iteration made the estimated likelihood jump wherever the number of refits changed, by up to 4.5e-10 on the Tanzania survey, whereas three refits are a smooth function of the parameters, as the theory of the certificate assumes, and jumped by at most 2e-12 there. The proposal at the start of a stage is still iterated to the tolerance. In a paired test on 127 simulated surveys with ten runs each, every run was certified with and without the change, the median ratio of the certificates was 1.000, the largest rise in the error was 0.002 standard errors, and the fits took 0.81 of the time. A refit that fails counts as a failure of the global proposal, as before. Each stage of mcml_history records refit_change, the largest change of a factor at the last of the three refits.

  • set_control_mcml() gains integrate_noise. With TRUE, a binomial or Poisson model with a nugget, with any link, integrates the nugget out of the likelihood of each location numerically, and certified MCML samples only the spatial effect and any unstructured random effects. The model, its parameters, its likelihood and predict() are unchanged, so the option changes only how the same maximum is found. The integral is tabled for each distinct pair of positives and trials on a grid of the linear predictor, by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature up to a nugget variance of 0.2 and the trapezium rule above it for the canonical links, and by the trapezium rule with a step set by the narrowest width of the integrand for a custom link, and read through a quintic Hermite interpolant. Records at a location with the same covariates, offset and random-effect levels are combined, and at a location that still has several records the nugget stays sampled. A nugget held at zero is held at exactly zero, where every record takes the plain kernel. On simulated surveys the integrated form kept 3 to 6 times as many effective draws at the same parameters. In this form a global iteration that stops at its limit of 500 refits with a last change below 0.01 is accepted, instead of sending the stage to the Laplace proposal. This is safe because the certificate rests on validation banks drawn after the proposal is fixed, so a nearly settled anchor changes how efficient the sampler is, not whether the estimate or its certificate is valid. On simulated surveys of 700 sites with a spatial variance of 5 the iteration often stopped just short of its tolerance of 1e-8, and the Laplace proposal then left almost no effective draws. The stages where this happened record stalled_anchors and stalled_change in mcml_history, summarised as mcml_stalled_anchors. The sampled form keeps its rule, so its fits are unchanged. The default of laplace_start becomes NULL, meaning TRUE for the sampled form and FALSE with integrate_noise = TRUE. check_fit() says at how many locations the nugget was integrated out, and suggests the option for a fit with a nugget variance of at least 0.1 that was not certified or whose weights have a heavy tail. Where the nugget variance is close to zero the likelihood is nearly flat along the nugget, and the integrated estimate of the nugget’s score is far noisier than the sampled one, so there the integrated form certified fewer fits (on simulated surveys of 700 sites, 5 against 12 of 21 runs below a nugget variance of 0.1, 68 against 28 of 75 above 0.3). With integrate_noise = "auto" both forms are built and each stage of the fit integrates the nugget out when its variance at the start of the stage is at least 0.1 and samples it otherwise, the first stage taking the variance from the Laplace estimate. Each stage records its form in mcml_history, the fit records them as mcml_noise_forms, and check_fit() reports them. With "auto" every validation bank is drawn in both forms, and the two estimates of the score are combined with weights inverse to their Monte Carlo covariances, so the certificate rests on the more precise form or on both. A bank whose importance weights have a Pareto k above 0.8 is left out of the combination, since a heavy tail can make its estimated covariance far too small. On 96 simulated surveys of 700 sites with nugget variances of 0.15 and 0.8, three runs each, the sampled form certified 124 of the 288 fits and "auto" 224. Among the fits with a Markov chain reference, "auto" had no error above the tolerance of 0.1 in the reference’s information (222 fits), against two for the sampled form (122). In every cell of the design it gave at least as many certificates with an error within the tolerance as the sampled form, and more in 31 of the 48 cells. It took 31 core-hours against 38. In a build before the replicate bank’s radius the sampled form certified 142 of the fits and the integrated form 213, and without the ceiling on k the combination certified 245, 9 of them with an error above the tolerance. The stages record the combination in combined of each validation bank in mcml_history. The extra check "radius" of check_fit() rebuilds its samples in the form of the nugget of the fit’s last stage, and where that stage combined the two forms it resamples banks in each form and combines them in pairs as the fit does, which takes about twice as long. "auto" is the default, so fits of binomial and Poisson models with a nugget change, while a model without a nugget is fitted as before.

  • integrate_noise now also integrates out re() terms whose levels lie within a single location, such as households in a village cluster, alongside the nugget. Records at a location with the same covariates, offset and random-effect levels are combined into one unit, and three rules decide each level and location. A level that holds a single unit is integrated out of that unit’s likelihood, with the variances of all such levels added, and at a location with a single unit so is the nugget. At a location with several units the nugget is integrated out as well when the units share their covariates and offset and differ only in levels that each hold a single unit, through an integral over the nugget of the units’ own integrals, tabled for each pattern of units and pair of variances in the same way as the records. At any other location the nugget stays sampled. Every other level stays sampled, including levels that span several locations and levels that hold units with different covariates, and a term can be integrated out at some levels and sampled at others. The integrated levels leave the latent vector, so the sampled dimension falls by one for each of them. A variance held at zero is held at exactly zero in this form, as the nugget is, and the test of a held variance takes the slope of a nested location’s likelihood in its inner variance directly. With "auto" a model with such a term is fitted as with TRUE, its re() terms and its nugget integrated out at every stage wherever the rules allow, while a model whose only such term is the nugget switches it by stage as before. check_fit() says for each term at how many levels it was integrated out and at how many it stayed sampled, and summary() gives them as integration in place of integrated_locations. The radius check and profile() rebuild the integrated form for such a fit. On 48 simulated surveys of 200 locations with about 800 households each, fitted three times in each form, TRUE, and so "auto", certified all 144 fits against 128 sampled, at a median bound of 0.022 against 0.063, in 9% of the sampled form’s time. Against MCMC references the median error was 0.011 against 0.017 sampled, and no fit was off by more than the tolerance. Switching the nugget alone with the households integrated certified 142 of 143, and on a survey whose nugget variance was zero two of its three runs ended without a certificate. On a survey built from malkenya’s households the bounds fell from about 0.08 sampled to 0.007 integrated. A model without such terms is fitted exactly as before.

  • The integral over the independent effects of a record or a location, which integrate_noise tables, no longer slows down as a variance grows. Records with no events, or with every trial an event, have a side where the likelihood is flat, and the trapezium rule walked across it a distance proportional to the standard deviation, so at the upper bound of the search for a log variance, 20, one evaluation took seconds to minutes, and a fit whose optimiser stepped there could run for hours. Such a stretch is now taken in closed form wherever the likelihood is linear across it, the steps of a location’s integral over its nugget grow with the standard deviation of its inner effects, and with a custom or named link the parts beyond the range on which the link is tabled, where its likelihood is constant, are taken in closed form as well. The search for the mode of the integrand now finds a mode far from the linear predictor, and the integral of a Poisson record whose linear predictor is in the hundreds is now right, where it overflowed. Up to a variance of about 100 the values are unchanged, and above it they agree with numerical integration to about 1e-10.

  • A Newton correction of a certified Monte Carlo maximum likelihood estimate that would take a variance or the spatial scale past the upper bound of the search is no longer applied. Such a correction follows a direction along which the likelihood is nearly flat. The fit keeps its estimate and is reported as not certified, with a warning, and check_fit() says why and suggests a larger max_samples. Before, the parameter was clamped at the bound and the certificate was computed there.

  • profile() of a binomial or Poisson fit now rebuilds the likelihood with the link of the fit. It used the logit or log link whatever link the fit had, so the profiles of a fit with a named link such as binomial("probit"), or with an inverse link given in invlink, were those of another model, and nothing warned of it. The fix does not change the profiles of fits with the logit and log links.

  • check_fit() gains extra, which names the checks that cost computing time, with "all" for every one, so that check_fit() is the one place to check a fit (#262). The first is "profile", the marginal profile likelihood from profile() of every covariance parameter of the fit, which are the spatial variance and scale, the nugget, an estimated measurement error variance and the variances of the random effects, but not the regression coefficients. Its row names each parameter whose profile is flat, so that its 95% interval is open at an end, or has a second maximum, and is then SUSPICIOUS, and is a PROBLEM when a point of a profile is above the estimate, which is then not the maximum likelihood estimate. cores runs the profiles in parallel, with the same results. Before the extra checks start, a message says how long they should take, from the time the fit took, the number of parameters and the cores. Each draws from a random number stream of its own after the seed of the fit, so the same call gives the same result, and the random number state of the session is left as it was. A profile already computed can be passed to check_fit() in profile, which moves there from plot() of the checks, and is used as it is, whatever parameters it covers. The checks returned keep the result of every check that ran with the numbers behind its finding, and the new summary() of the checks gives them, with the certificate and draws of each stage and the full results of the extra checks, while print() still gives the verdict. plot() of the checks gains which to choose its panels, draws only what was computed, and says which extra check would compute a panel that is missing. Each profiled parameter has its own panel, such as "profile_phi", and which = "profile" draws them all. The print of a fit without extra checks is unchanged.

  • check_fit() gains the extra check "radius" for binomial and Poisson fits, which predicts how often the radius in the bound on the Monte Carlo error is too small (#262). The radius is estimated from the certification draws themselves, which can miss the rare draws of large importance weight. Sixteen short Markov chains on the latent effects reach those draws, and samples of certification draws resampled from them and a fresh sample of the fit’s size give the rate at which the error that the radius allows for exceeds it, with a 95% interval, against the 5% of the bound. On 35 simulated binomial and Poisson surveys the prediction was within a factor of 1.65 of the rate measured on independent samples. Outside binomial fits with the logit link it is read with a margin of 15%, since it ran low on the Poisson surveys. The row is SUSPICIOUS when the radius, with that margin, would have to widen for the rate to be 5%, and then gives the bound with the radius so widened. The chains can miss a separate mode of the latent effects, so OK is not a proof. The check should take about twice as long as the fit, and draws from the streams 9500 to 9502 after the seed of the fit. plot() of the checks gains the panel "radius", the error of resampled samples against the radius the fit uses for them, whose subtitle gives the predicted rate first.

  • print() of the checks from check_fit() now gives a check that needs a look in full with its fix, and a check that is OK on one line with its finding in a few words, and ends by pointing to summary(), which now gives every finding in full before the numbers behind it (#262). A fix that a costly check would settle names it, check_fit(fit, extra = "profile") for a scale that may be weakly identified and for other maxima, and check_fit(fit, extra = "radius") for heavy-tailed importance weights, or points to the row of that check when it ran. plot() of the checks gains two panels drawn from what the fit recorded. "held_variances" shows the slope of the log-likelihood at each variance held at zero with its interval of 2.58 standard errors, the test of the fit, and "screen" shows the screen of short scales of the check for other maxima, the log-likelihood estimated at each short scale and the exact lower bound there, against the estimate and the limit with independent location effects. Each says why when it has nothing to show. A fit now records the exact bound at each scale of the screen and, with the spatial variance at zero and a nugget, over the scales and spatial shares, where it kept only the largest, and summary() of the checks gives them. Estimates and the decisions of a fit are unchanged.

  • Certified MCML no longer stops with “the optimiser returned non-finite parameter values” when the search for the conditional mode of the latent effects goes wrong. Each search starts from the mode found at the parameter values tried before it. On a simulated survey at 1% prevalence a search had accepted steps to -507, where the curvature of the logit link underflows to 0 / 0, and the next search started there. No step was then accepted, and the search returned its start as the mode, with a Hessian that was not a number, as if it had converged. 15 of the 48 searches of the Laplace step were broken this way, which moved the Laplace estimate, and the importance distribution at that estimate was not a number, so that every log weight was missing. A step to a point where the likelihood terms are not finite is no longer accepted. A search fails when its terms, its Newton step or its Hessian are not finite, or when no step increases the objective at a point that is not a mode, and a failed search from the previous mode is repeated from zero, so the next search starts from a mode that was found. An importance distribution that is not finite is an error, which gives that parameter value no weight, as other failures to build one do. check_fit() reports how many searches started again from zero. The three runs on that survey that stopped now fit, within 0.05 standard errors of a Markov chain reference, and two are certified. The third reaches the largest budget of 16,000 draws with a bound of 0.18. Fits whose searches never went wrong are unchanged, as on two other surveys of the same study.

  • parametric_bootstrap() simulates datasets from a Gaussian, binomial or Poisson fit at its estimate, refits the model to each from the estimate, and reports for each parameter the bootstrap median, bias, standard error and percentile and bias-corrected (BC) intervals. The BC interval corrects for the downward bias of the estimators of the spatial variance and the scale, which shifts percentile intervals the wrong way. Each replicate has its own seed, 10000 apart from the next so that no two replicates share a Monte Carlo stream, and the results are the same for any number of cores. Failed refits are recorded instead of stopping the bootstrap. plot() draws a histogram of each parameter with the estimate and both intervals.

  • plot() of a profile now shows the relative profile log-likelihood, the profile log-likelihood minus its maximum, which is 0 at the estimate and negative elsewhere, so that the cut-off of a 95% interval is at -1.92 instead of 3.84. scale = "deviance" draws the profile deviance as before. The panel of a joint profile is titled “Joint profile”, and its legend calls the two ridges “best y for each x” and “best x for each y”, since the axes name the parameters. plot() of a parametric bootstrap draws each histogram on the natural scale of the parameter, and gains log_scale = TRUE for the logarithmic axis of the variances and the scale that it used before. Logarithmic axes of both plots are labelled with plain numbers, such as 0.00001 and 1,000 instead of 1e-05 and 1e+03. profile() of a binomial or Poisson fit labels the parameters as summary(), parametric_bootstrap() and profile() of a Gaussian fit do, for example “Spatial process var.” instead of “Spatial variance”. The printed intervals of a profile have 4 significant digits, with the lower and upper ends of each interval under a common heading, so that the table fits 80 characters.

Predictions

  • Grids created by create_grid() now have the class RiskMap_grid before data.frame, as vctrs requires of data frame subclasses. dplyr verbs such as filter() previously failed with an error on these grids and on the predictions made from them.
  • create_grid() no longer raises an error when boundaries is in longitude/latitude; like glgpm(), it now automatically reprojects to an appropriate UTM zone and reports the conversion with a message.
  • The old three-stage prediction interface has been replaced by predict.RiskMap(). Prediction locations, predictors, offsets, grouping variables and weights are supplied together in one sf object. Supplying boundaries requests blockwise joint prediction and areal aggregation; grids created by create_grid() use exact fractional cell coverage. Location- and area-level predictions support exceedance probabilities and named draw-by-draw transformations for additional scientific targets. Response predictions can be standardized over a common empirical or counterfactual reference population, with optional population weights.
  • Gaussian prediction uses a stable reduced covariance solve, avoiding cancellation with small measurement-error variances while retaining the same conditional model.
  • predict() gains parameter_uncertainty (default FALSE) and parameter_draws (default 50). When requested, parameters are drawn from the approximate sampling distribution of the estimate and, for each draw, the latent effects are sampled at that value with a short run of the same Langevin sampler used for plug-in prediction. The pooled draws give intervals, exceedance probabilities and areal summaries that also reflect parameter uncertainty, which matters for small or low-prevalence surveys.
  • The Langevin sampler of the latent effects, used by predict() and by the final draw of glgpm(), is faster, most of all with re() terms. Its Laplace preconditioner is factored through the Schur complement of the re() term with most levels, and each iteration applies that factor without the prior precision, so that it costs two triangular solves of the size of the locations and passes over the records, instead of dense algebra in every location and re() level. The conditional mode is found by Newton’s method with the same factor instead of nlminb() with a dense Hessian, and links other than the canonical ones, including named links such as binomial("cloglog"), run in the compiled chain. For a chain of 12,000 iterations a call takes 0.16 s instead of 0.28 s for 200 sites with one record each, 1.8 s instead of 18 s for 1,000 sites, 0.5 s instead of 19 s for 200 sites with about 800 households as re() levels, and 4 s instead of 13 minutes for a survey of 46 clusters with 4,868 households. The chain now starts from a draw of the Laplace approximation rather than at the mode. From the mode a chain in many dimensions accepted almost nothing until its step had shrunk, while from a draw it is in its stationary spread at once. The step size kept after burn-in is the geometric mean of the tuned step over the second half of burn-in, which keeps the acceptance rate closer to its target, and a long chain can be interrupted. With parameter_uncertainty = TRUE the mode at each parameter draw is found by the same search, started from the mode at the previous draw, instead of the dense Laplace approximation of the fitting engine, and each chain keeps the step tuned at the estimate with a burn-in of 100 iterations instead of 500, so that predict() takes 10 s instead of 80 s for the 200 sites with households. A seed still gives the same results every time, but they differ from those the same seed gave before, although they follow the same distribution.
  • set_control_mcmc() keeps 2,000 draws by default instead of 1,000, with n_sim = 22000 and the same burn-in of 2,000 iterations and thinning by 10. glgpm() stores these draws and predict() reuses them, so the Monte Carlo error of predictions is about 1.4 times smaller. Predictions on a grid hold twice as many draws in memory and take two to two and a half times as long, for example 8 s instead of 4 s for a new chain on the 8,740 cells of tz_covariates. Gaussian models also take 2,000 independent draws by default, including with parameter_uncertainty = TRUE, which took 12,000, and with set_control_mcmc(linear_model = TRUE), which also took 12,000.
  • plot() maps the output of predict(). Default colours depend on what the map shows: a calm-to-alarm palette for predicted levels, a single neutral hue for uncertainty (sd, cv, interval_width), a blue-to-red palette centred at 50% for exceedance probabilities and a palette centred at zero for signed effects. The legend title names the quantity (for example “Mean prevalence” for binomial models) and probabilities are labelled as percentages. spatial_scale = "both" draws locations and areas side by side with a shared colour scale, several summaries can be drawn in one call, breaks gives a binned map, and boundaries supplied to predict() are outlined automatically. print() lists what a prediction contains and how to map it. predict() output now records response_name.
  • create_grid() gains keep. keep = "overlap" keeps every cell that overlaps the boundary, including edge cells whose centre lies outside, so that totals such as population along a coastline are not lost. The grid metadata now also records the study boundary.
  • Prediction maps draw grid cells as squares clipped to the grid’s study boundary, so further sf layers (for example survey locations) can be added to a map in any coordinate reference system.
